questions.question: A large job has independent tasks with unpredictable durations. Which swarm feature distributes work without a central dispatcher?
options: A single supervisor assigns every task after each worker finishes
One agent holds all state and runs every executor serially
Each task waits for all earlier task results
Workers pull the next available task from a shared queue
questions.explanation: Each idle worker pulls the next available item from a shared queue, so variable durations are balanced without a central dispatcher assigning every completion. A supervisor could rebalance tasks too, but it would violate the stated no-central-dispatcher condition.

questions.question: Which task is a good fit for a decentralized worker swarm?
options: Many independent items with throughput more important than strict order
A research task that needs one coherent global plan
A pipeline where each step needs the immediately prior result
A workflow where every decision needs a single audit owner
questions.explanation: A decentralized swarm suits many independent items when throughput matters more than a single global plan. A multi-step pipeline has ordering dependencies, so independent pulls can start work before required inputs exist.

questions.question: A swarm processes a step before the task that produces its input. Which task property makes the architecture a poor fit?
options: There are several independent classifications
The work items vary in duration
Workers can subscribe to task types
The workflow has ordering dependencies
questions.explanation: If a step needs an earlier result, task order is a dependency constraint; queue availability alone does not guarantee its producer has finished. Variable duration and task-type subscriptions do not fix that prerequisite relation.

questions.question: What queue policy can reduce starvation of long-running tasks?
options: Always pick the task with the shortest estimated runtime
Allow fast-task producers to enqueue without back-pressure
Priority aging that raises a task's priority as it waits
Drop any task that remains in the queue too long
questions.explanation: Priority aging raises the effective priority of work as its wait grows, preventing fast short tasks from indefinitely passing a long one. Always choosing the shortest estimate can repeatedly defer the slow job.

questions.question: The swarm demo uses an in-memory queue. What production property is missing if workers may crash?
options: A random ordering of task ids
Durable storage so queued tasks survive worker failure
A global model shared by all executors
A longer system prompt shared by every worker
questions.explanation: A process-local queue disappears when its worker process exits, so recovery needs a durable queue or store that preserves pending tasks. A shared model changes what workers compute, not whether queued work survives a crash.

questions.question: A fixed assignment gives one worker all the slow jobs while other workers finish early. Why can shared-queue pulling improve wall time?
options: A queue sorts all tasks by their final result
The queue makes every slow task finish faster
The coordinator forces every worker to handle the same job
Available workers take remaining work instead of waiting idle
questions.explanation: Dynamic queue pulling lets a worker that finishes early claim remaining work rather than sit idle behind a worker’s fixed batch of slow jobs. The queue balances assignments; it does not accelerate the execution of any one slow task.
